pedagogy.summary: Naming the parts of a circle (radius, diameter, circumference) and knowing the diameter is twice the radius is taught best by grounding each term in its DEFINING PROPERTY — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a line through the centre from edge to edge, the circumference is the distance all the way round — rather than by rote labels. Drawing and measuring many circles of different sizes and tabulating radius against diameter lets pupils discover the invariant d = 2r for themselves, and practising the conversion in BOTH directions guards against the pervasive radius/diameter swap.
bestPractices: Anchor each term in its defining property: a radius touches the centre; a diameter passes through the centre; the circumference is the perimeter (distance around).
Draw and measure several circles of different sizes and tabulate radius vs diameter, so pupils see d = 2r holds at every scale.
Practise conversion in both directions — diameter from radius AND radius from diameter — and monitor for confusion between the two (NCTM).
Label parts on circles in varied positions and surface the longest-chord property (the diameter is the longest line across).
Provide a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and require pupils to use the terms when they reason.
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle: centre, radius, diameter, circumference
Radius vs diameter vs an off-centre chord, contrasted
A radius/diameter table across several circle sizes
String wrapped round a circle to show the circumference as a length
commonMisconceptions: Swaps radius and diameter, or substitutes a diameter where a radius is needed — the 'half/twice' error (NCTM).
Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or draws a radius/diameter that does not reach or pass through the centre.
Applies the conversion in the wrong direction (doubles when it should halve), or thinks the radius equals the diameter.

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) learn to name and identify the radius, diameter and circumference of a circle by their DEFINING PROPERTIES — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a straight line from edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across), and the circumference is the distance all the way around — and to apply d = 2r in both directions. The core work is drawing and measuring many circles, tabulating radius against diameter so the invariant d = 2r is discovered rather than told, and practising conversion both ways to guard against the pervasive radius/diameter swap. Several complementary media (dynamic manipulation, paper-and-string measurement, a labelled reference, and a short conversion check) each support a different part of this objective.

activities.title: Measure many circles and discover d = 2r
feedback: If a pupil's pairs don't come out close to double, check that the diameter was drawn through the centre and that both were measured along a straight line — an off-centre line is shorter and will break the pattern.
Prompt: 'Does your doubling pattern still hold for your biggest circle and your smallest circle?' to surface that the relationship is scale-independent.
If a pupil writes the names interchangeably, ask them to point to where each line starts and ends relative to the centre.
activities.rationale: Grounding each term in its defining property and tabulating radius against diameter across sizes lets pupils see d = 2r hold at every scale, which the curriculum expects pupils to know and the geometry research links to moving beyond naming toward defining properties.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference, and know that the diameter is twice the radius; the non-statutory guidance expresses this as d = 2 × r.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Draw several circles of clearly different sizes (small, medium, large).
For each circle, mark the centre, draw a radius from the centre to the edge and a diameter from edge to edge through the centre.
Measure the radius and the diameter of each circle and record them in a two-column table (radius | diameter).
Look across the table and describe the pattern you notice between the radius and the diameter.
State the relationship in your own words and as d = 2 × r.
activities.intendedInsight: Across every size of circle, the diameter is exactly twice the radius. Pupils' own measurements will come out close to double, allowing for small measuring errors, so they can see the pattern holding for themselves rather than memorising a rule.

activities.title: Which line is longest? Predict then measure
feedback: Many pupils pick a long-looking slanted line; after measuring, point out that the through-centre line always wins, which is why the diameter is defined by the centre, not by looking long.
If a pupil labels an off-centre chord a diameter, have them check whether it passes through the marked centre.
Fold a paper circle in half (and again) to locate the centre, then confirm which drawn lines actually pass through it.
activities.rationale: Predicting before measuring makes the reasoning visible and the counterexample (an off-centre chord) directly tests the through-centre defining property rather than surface appearance, countering prototype-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: On a circle with the centre marked, draw several straight lines from edge to edge — some passing through the centre and some not.
Before measuring, PREDICT which line is the longest and write down why you think so.
Measure each line and compare with your prediction.
Decide which lines pass through the centre (diameters) and which do not (other chords), and explain the difference using the word 'centre'.
activities.intendedInsight: The longest straight line across a circle is always the one through the centre — the diameter — so a line that misses the centre is a shorter chord, not a diameter. The pre-stated reason is what reveals a pupil's thinking.

activities.title: Convert both ways and reason aloud
feedback: Worked check: a radius of 4.5 cm gives a diameter of 9 cm because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). A diameter of 10 cm gives a radius of 5 cm because the radius is half the diameter.
If a pupil gives 2.25 cm as the diameter of a 4.5 cm radius, they halved instead of doubling — return to the measured table showing the diameter is always the larger, doubled value.
Require the pupil to name which quantity is which before computing, so a radius isn't treated as a diameter.
activities.rationale: Practising conversion in both directions and requiring reasoning with correct vocabulary targets the flagged radius/diameter confusion and supports fluent, justified use of the terms.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Given a radius (e.g. 4.5 cm), work out the diameter and state how you did it.
Given a diameter (e.g. 10 cm), work out the radius and state how you did it.
For each, say in words whether you doubled or halved and why.
Use a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and use the correct term in each explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting diameter-from-radius and radius-from-diameter are different directions of the same relationship; knowing which to double and which to halve, with a reason, prevents the half/twice swap.

activities.title: Feel the circumference as a length
feedback: If a pupil calls a straight line across the circle 'the circumference', have them trace the edge with a finger: the circumference is the whole way round.
Compare the straightened string length with the diameter drawn straight across to reinforce that they measure different things.
activities.rationale: A tactile wrap-and-straighten activity is intended to make the circumference concrete as a go-around length, addressing the confusion between circumference and a straight measurement across. Proposed as a hands-on scaffold; its effectiveness is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Wrap a length of string once around the edge of a circle, mark where it meets, then straighten it against a ruler to measure the distance around.
Run a finger all the way around the edge and say in your own words what the circumference is.
Contrast this with a straight line drawn across the circle and explain why the circumference is not a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: The circumference is the distance all the way around the edge — a curved length — not a straight line across the circle.

activities.title: Dynamic circle: watch d = 2r hold as the circle resizes (optional screen scaffold)
feedback: Live readout feedback: as the pupil stretches the circle, the diameter reading stays at twice the radius (the last digit may differ slightly if the display rounds), so the relationship can be observed across scales.
When a dragged line misses the centre and is refused the 'diameter' label, prompt: 'What do you need to change so it becomes a diameter?'
Pair this with the paper-and-ruler measuring so the relationship is grounded in real measurement, not only an on-screen readout.
activities.rationale: A dynamic, draggable model lets the invariant be experienced across many sizes in quick succession and can enforce the through-centre property via snapping/labelling; a static labelled reference states d = 2r but cannot show it varying. Offered as a complement to, not a replacement for, hands-on measuring; its efficacy relative to other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Drag a point to make the circle bigger and smaller and watch a live readout of the radius and the diameter.
Notice whether the diameter readout always shows twice the radius as the size changes.

Drag the endpoint of a line inside the circle; observe that it is labelled 'diameter — the longest line across' only when it passes through the centre, and is refused the label when it misses the centre.
Say what stays the same (d = 2r) and what must be true for a line to be a diameter (it passes through the centre).
activities.intendedInsight: The 2× relationship is invariant across every size, and only a through-centre line earns the name 'diameter' — both the invariant and the defining property made visible together.

activities.title: Labelled circle reference (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Reveal-on-tap can confirm each term's defining property as a reference, but d = 2r is stated here, not discovered — use it alongside the measuring activity.
Varying the position of the labelled parts guards against pupils only recognising a standard horizontal diameter.
If a pupil can label a standard diagram but slips on a slanted or off-centre line, return to the defining-property test (does it pass through the centre?).
activities.rationale: A clear labelled reference with varied positions supports the vocabulary and surfaces the longest-chord property; presenting shapes in varied positions counters prototype-based recognition. This is a reference scaffold and cannot by itself build the measured discovery of the invariant.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Study a labelled circle showing centre, radius, diameter and circumference.
Reveal or read each term's defining property: radius = centre to edge; diameter = edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across); circumference = the distance all the way round.
Label parts yourself on circles drawn in varied positions and orientations, including ones where the diameter is slanted.
Match each term to its definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Each circle part is identified by its defining property and position relative to the centre, not by a fixed picture orientation.

constraints: A static labelled diagram or reveal-on-tap reference states d = 2r but does not let pupils see it vary across sizes; pair it with hands-on drawing and measuring so the invariant is genuinely discovered.

A label/match/slider conversion check can verify vocabulary and the d = 2r computation but does not by itself build the defining-property understanding; use it as a check after the measuring and reasoning activities.
Recognition-only responses (matching terms to a standard diagram) do not elicit independent construction; require pupils to draw, measure, convert both ways, and justify.
Present diameters and radii in varied positions (including slanted and non-standard) so pupils do not over-rely on a horizontal prototype.
Always insist pupils state WHY (which line passes through the centre, whether they doubled or halved); the reason is what distinguishes understanding from a lucky guess.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 3-D environment as 'adding nothing' for a planar concept. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A planar concept is naturally well-served by 2-D media, but no universal 'adds nothing' claim is made here.

The source stated conversation is 'poor' for this concept. This is not a general pedagogical law; spoken justification is used throughout (predict-and-explain, reason-aloud conversion) as part of teaching, not only assessment. The medium-ranking boilerplate was removed.
The 'diameter is the longest line across (longest chord)' property is stated correctly for a circle and is used as a measurable, verifiable prediction task.

Self-audit of the worked conversions: radius 4.5 cm → diameter 9 cm (2 × 4.5) is correct; the distractor 2.25 cm correctly models halving instead of doubling; diameter 10 cm → radius 5 cm is correct. No arithmetic errors found.

The circumference string activity and the circumference-vs-straight-line confusion it targets come from the pedagogy/assessment material, not from the cited sources; its sourceClaims were set to [] and the rationale hedged accordingly, as no source establishes the method's effectiveness.
All sourceClaims were re-checked to be verbatim copies of the three original sources[].claim strings; this addresses the prior validation failure caused by a non-matching claim string.

assess.poeTask: Draw several straight lines from edge to edge across a circle, some through the marked centre and some not, and ask the pupil to PREDICT which line is longest before measuring — and to say why. Many pick a long-looking slanted chord. Then measure: the longest is always the line through the centre — the diameter. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part; the result forces the defining property that a diameter must pass through the centre and is the longest chord.
probeDeeper: If I make the circle twice as big, is the diameter still twice the radius? Why?
This line goes across the circle but not through the centre — is it a diameter? Why not?
A circle's diameter is 10 cm — what is its radius, and how did you work it out?
Which straight line across a circle is the longest, and where must it pass?
assess.correctAnswer: The diameter is 9 cm, because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). The centre-to-edge line is the radius and the edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter; a radius goes from the centre to the edge and a diameter passes through the centre, so the third line is neither (it is a chord) because it does not pass through the centre.

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps radius and diameter or applies the relationship the wrong way — the 'half/twice' error (halves when it should double)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw and measure circles and tabulate radius against diameter to see the diameter is always double the radius; practise both conversion directions
errorPatterns.distractor: 2.25 cm (halved the radius instead of doubling it)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the diameter as 2.25 cm, or labels the centre-to-edge line as the diameter

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or a line to the edge as a radius, ignoring the centre — the defining property
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold a paper circle to find the centre; only a line through the centre is a diameter (and it is the longest line across), and a radius must start at the centre
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the off-centre chord as the diameter, or draws a 'radius' that does not reach the centre

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the circumference with a straight measurement — calls a diameter or a line across 'the circumference'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a finger all the way round the edge — the circumference is the distance around, not a straight line across
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a straight line as the circumference

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms interchangeably or halves/doubles in the wrong direction; treats any line across the circle as a diameter.
responseLevels.full: States and applies d = 2r in both directions with a reason, identifies parts by their defining properties (radius from the centre, diameter through the centre, circumference around), rejects an off-centre chord as a diameter, and knows the relationship holds at any size.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one way (e.g. radius to diameter) and labels a standard diagram, but slips on the reverse conversion or on a non-standard/off-centre line — knows the names without the defining property.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A circle has a radius of 4.5 cm. What is its diameter, and how do you know? Then look at this diagram of a circle with its centre marked and three straight lines drawn on it: one from the centre to the edge, one from edge to edge passing through the centre, and one from edge to edge that does NOT pass through the centre. Which line is the radius, which is the diameter, and how can you tell?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier separates a pupil who applies d = 2r with understanding from one who guesses or halves. The diagram forces the defining-property test: a pupil who thinks any line across the circle is a diameter picks the off-centre chord, whereas a pupil who knows the property rejects it because it misses the centre. Together the tiers catch both the half/twice swap and the through-centre confusion.
